# Three-phase six-step inverter

*Lecture 3 · EEU 08104 Power Electronics Design*

The **three-phase six-step** (or **quasi-square-wave**) inverter is a voltage-source inverter widely used in commercial adjustable-speed AC motor drives. A third leg (half bridge) is added to the single-phase bridge, and the output terminals A, B and C feed a three-phase motor. It has **6 switches** and **6 feedback diodes**.

## Operation

- The operation is essentially the same as the single-phase bridge. **Each switch is on for 180°** and each output terminal is connected for half a period to the positive rail and for half to the negative rail.
- A three-phase output is obtained by keeping a **120° displacement** between the switching sequences of the three legs.
- This gives the firing order shown by the switch numbering: **SW1, SW2, SW3, SW4, SW5, SW6**, each switched on at regular intervals of **60°** (0° S1, 60° S2, 120° S3, 180° S4, 240° S5, 300° S6, 360° S1 again).
- Leg A: S1 (top) and S4 (bottom). Leg B: S3 and S6. Leg C: S5 and S2.

The pole voltages are ±V<sub>d</sub>/2 square waves 120° apart; the line voltage v<sub>AB</sub> = v<sub>AO</sub> − v<sub>BO</sub> is a quasi-square wave (120° on, 60° off); the phase voltage of a star load has six steps of V<sub>d</sub>/3 and 2V<sub>d</sub>/3.</figcaption></figure>

## Pole voltages

Taking the DC midpoint O as reference, $v_{AO}$, $v_{BO}$ and $v_{CO}$ are square waves of amplitude $V_d/2$, each 120° behind the previous one. A square wave has only odd harmonics:

$$v_{AO} = \frac{4}{\pi}\cdot\frac{V_d}{2}\left[\sin\omega t + \frac13\sin3\omega t + \frac15\sin5\omega t + \frac17\sin7\omega t + \cdots\right]$$

$$v_{BO} = \frac{4}{\pi}\cdot\frac{V_d}{2}\left[\sin\left(\omega t - \frac{2\pi}{3}\right) + \frac13\sin3\left(\omega t - \frac{2\pi}{3}\right) + \frac15\sin5\left(\omega t - \frac{2\pi}{3}\right) + \cdots\right]$$

**Assignment (from the slides): write the Fourier expression for $v_{CO}$.** It is the same series shifted by a further 120°:

$$v_{CO} = \frac{2V_d}{\pi}\left[\sin\left(\omega t - \frac{4\pi}{3}\right) + \frac13\sin3\left(\omega t - \frac{4\pi}{3}\right) + \frac15\sin5\left(\omega t - \frac{4\pi}{3}\right) + \cdots\right]$$

Note that the third harmonics of the three pole voltages are **in phase** ($3 \times 120° = 360°$).

## Line voltages

$$v_{AB} = v_{AO} - v_{BO}, \qquad v_{BC} = v_{BO} - v_{CO}, \qquad v_{CA} = v_{CO} - v_{AO}$$

Each line voltage is a quasi-square wave: $+V_d$ for 120°, zero for 60°, $-V_d$ for 120°, zero for 60°. Because the triplen harmonics cancel in the subtraction, the line voltage **contains no third harmonic or multiples of it**:

$$v_{ab} = \sum_{n = 1,3,5,\ldots}\frac{4V_d}{n\pi}\cos\frac{n\pi}{6}\sin n\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

and $v_{bc}$, $v_{ca}$ are the same shifted by 120° and 240°. With the time origin moved by $\pi/6$:

$$v_{ab} = \frac{2\sqrt3V_d}{\pi}\left[\sin\omega t - \frac15\sin5\omega t - \frac17\sin7\omega t + \frac{1}{11}\sin11\omega t + \frac{1}{13}\sin13\omega t - \cdots\right]$$

**rms values**

$$V_L = \left[\frac{2}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi/3}V_d^2\,d(\omega t)\right]^{1/2} = \sqrt{\frac23}V_d = 0.8165V_d$$

$$V_{Ln} = \frac{4V_d}{\sqrt2n\pi}\cos\frac{n\pi}{6}, \qquad V_{L1} = \frac{4V_d}{\sqrt2\pi}\cos30° = 0.7797V_d$$

## Phase (line-to-neutral) voltages

With a balanced star-connected load, the phase voltage has **six distinct steps per cycle**, hence the name six-step. In each 60° interval three switches are closed, and the load is two resistors in parallel in series with the third. For the first interval (S1, S5, S6 closed), A and C are on the positive rail and B on the negative:

$$R_{eq} = R + \frac{R}{2} = \frac32R, \qquad I = \frac{V_d}{3R/2} = \frac{2V_d}{3R}$$

$$v_{BN} = -\frac{2V_d}{3R}R = -\frac23V_d, \qquad v_{AN} = v_{CN} = \frac{2V_d}{3R}\cdot\frac{R}{2} = \frac13V_d$$

| Interval | Switches on | $v_{AN}$ | $v_{BN}$ | $v_{CN}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0°–60° | 5, 6, 1 | $V_d/3$ | $-2V_d/3$ | $V_d/3$ |
| 60°–120° | 6, 1, 2 | $2V_d/3$ | $-V_d/3$ | $-V_d/3$ |
| 120°–180° | 1, 2, 3 | $V_d/3$ | $V_d/3$ | $-2V_d/3$ |
| 180°–240° | 2, 3, 4 | $-V_d/3$ | $2V_d/3$ | $-V_d/3$ |
| 240°–300° | 3, 4, 5 | $-2V_d/3$ | $V_d/3$ | $V_d/3$ |
| 300°–360° | 4, 5, 6 | $-V_d/3$ | $-V_d/3$ | $2V_d/3$ |

**Assignment (from the slides): sketch $v_{BN}$ and $v_{CN}$.** Read them from the table: each has the same six-step shape as $v_{AN}$, $v_{BN}$ delayed by 120° and $v_{CN}$ by 240°.

**rms phase voltage:**

$$V_{ph} = \frac{V_L}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt2}{3}V_d = 0.4714V_d$$

**Fourier series:**

$$v_{an}(t) = \frac{2V_d}{\pi}\left(\sin\omega t + \sum_{n = 2,4,6,\ldots}\frac{1}{3n \pm 1}\sin(3n \pm 1)\omega t\right) = \frac{2V_d}{\pi}\left(\sin\omega t + \frac15\sin5\omega t + \frac17\sin7\omega t + \frac{1}{11}\sin11\omega t + \cdots\right)$$

so the rms fundamental phase voltage is $\dfrac{2V_d}{\sqrt2\pi} = 0.45V_d$ ($= 0.7797V_d/\sqrt3$).

## Why PWM

The six-step inverter needs only simple control, but its output voltage can only be changed by changing $V_d$, for example with a phase-controlled rectifier in front of it. When the DC source cannot be varied, or the losses of that extra stage cannot be tolerated, the **inverter itself** must vary the output voltage. That is done with **pulse-width modulation**, covered next.
